questions.text: What is a function?
options: An independently defined block of code that is called by name
A block of code that can only be called through an object
A variable that stores a class
A copy of a class with its own values
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 1: a function is an independently defined block of code that is called by name. It isn't encapsulated in any other code.

questions.text: How is a method different from a function?
options: A method can't be called by itself; it depends on the object it's defined in
A method can't take arguments
A method is defined with method instead of def
A method runs automatically when the script starts
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2: “A method, however, cannot be called by itself. It is dependent on the object in which it is defined.” You call it through the instance, e.g. myClass.method1Name(). Both are defined with def.

questions.text: Which line correctly defines a function named functionName that takes no arguments?
options: def functionName():
def functionName:
function functionName():
def functionName()
questions.explanation: A def needs parentheses (even when empty) and a colon. Part 2, Step 1's pseudo-code writes def functionName:, which Python rejects with SyntaxError: expected '(' — checked by running it.
questions.warning: Upon double checking, the lab's pseudo-code def functionName: isn't valid Python — it's missing the ().

questions.text: In the lab's method pseudo-code, how are the methods called?
options: Through the instance, with a dot: myClass.method1Name()
By name alone: method1Name()
Through the class keyword: class.method1Name()
They run automatically when the class is instantiated
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2: the class is instantiated as myClass, then each method is called on it with myClass.methodName(). Calling myLocation() by itself in this lab's script gives NameError: name 'myLocation' is not defined.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to complete the myCity function so it prints I live in Austin.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step b: def myCity(city): defines the function with the argument city, and the print joins it into the sentence.

questions.text: What does myCity.py print?
questions.context:
def myCity(city):
     print("I live in " + city + ".")

myCity("Austin")
myCity("Tokyo")
myCity("Salzburg")
options:
I live in Austin.
I live in Tokyo.
I live in Salzburg.

I live in city.
I live in city.
I live in city.
I live in Salzburg.
I live in AustinTokyoSalzburg.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step d: each call passes a different value for city, so the sentence prints three times with each city name. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What is a Python class used for?
options: To create objects that have properties and methods
To group several scripts into one file
To install packages into a virtual environment
To run code only once when the script starts
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1: “A Python class is used to create objects that have properties and methods.”

questions.text: When does a class's __init__() method run?
options: Every time the class is instantiated
Only when you call obj.__init__() yourself
Once, when the class is defined
When the script ends
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1: “The __init__() function is always initiated when a class is instantiated.” Location("Tomas", "Portugal") runs it with those values.

questions.text: Every Python class must explicitly define an __init__() method.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1: classes typically include an explicitly defined __init__(), “although you can create a class without defining one.”

questions.text: The lab sometimes calls it the __init__() “function”. Why is it technically a method?
options: Because it's defined inside, and depends on, the class
Because its name starts with underscores
Because it takes no arguments
Because it returns a value
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1 note: “Although it is sometimes called the __init__() function, it is dependent on the class. Therefore, it is technically a method.”

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to complete the Location class's constructor.
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1c: def __init__(self, name, country):, then each value is stored on the instance with self.name = name and self.country = country.

questions.text: What does the self parameter refer to?
options: The current instance of the class
The Python interpreter
The file the class is saved in
The method being called
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1c: “The self parameter is a reference to the current instance of the class itself.” By convention it's the first parameter. Through it, self.name and self.country are stored on that particular object, so loc1 and loc2 each keep their own values.

questions.text: The first parameter of a method has to be spelled self, or Python raises an error.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1c: “By convention, the first parameter is called self.” It's a convention, not a keyword — any name works, but everyone uses self.

questions.text: Which line creates a Location object called loc?
options: loc = Location("Your_Name", "Your_Country")
loc = new Location("Your_Name", "Your_Country")
Location loc = ("Your_Name", "Your_Country")
loc = Location.__init__("Your_Name", "Your_Country")
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1d: you instantiate by calling the class with the values its __init__() needs. Python has no new keyword, and you don't pass self yourself.

questions.text: What happens if you instantiate Location with only one value?
options: A TypeError — __init__() is missing the required argument country
country is set to None
country is set to an empty string
"Tomas" is used for both name and country
questions.explanation: name and country are required class variables (Part 4, Step 1d), so leaving one out raises TypeError: ... __init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'country'. Verified by running it.

questions.text: After loc = Location("Your_Name", "Your_Country"), what does this print?
options:
Your_Name
Your_Country

name
country

self.name
self.country
An AttributeError
questions.explanation: Part 4, Steps 1e and 1g: the dot reads the values __init__() stored on the instance. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What does print(type(loc)) output in myLocation.py?
options: <class '__main__.Location'>
<class 'type'>
<class 'object'>
Location
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1g: <class '__main__.Location'> — loc's type is the Location class, defined in the script being run (__main__). Verified by running it.

questions.text: print(type(loc)) showing <class '__main__.Location'> means loc is itself a class.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: type() tells you what class an object belongs to, so the output means loc is an instance (object) of Location. A class itself has type type: print(type(Location)) gives <class 'type'>, and isinstance(loc, Location) is True — both checked by running them.
questions.warning: Upon double checking, Part 4, Step 1f's wording (“verify the loc is indeed a class”) is loose: loc is an instance of the Location class, not a class.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to define the myLocation method so it can read the values set in __init__().
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 2c: the method is given the self parameter “so that the new method can access the variables defined in the __init__() function”, through self.name and self.country.

questions.text: After adding the myLocation method (with no instantiation code yet), running the script prints nothing.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 2e: “You will not get any output yet.” Defining a class and its methods doesn't run them; nothing prints until you create an instance and call the method.

questions.text: What does this print?
options: Hi, my name is Tomas and I live in Portugal.
Hi, my name is self.name and I live in self.country.
Tomas Portugal
Nothing — myLocation() has to be wrapped in print()
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 3b. The method does the printing itself, so calling it is enough. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What does print(loc1.myLocation()) output?
options:
Hi, my name is Tomas and I live in Portugal.
None
Hi, my name is Tomas and I live in Portugal.

Hi, my name is Tomas and I live in Portugal.
Hi, my name is Tomas and I live in Portugal.
None
questions.explanation: myLocation() prints its sentence but has no return, so it returns None — which the outer print() then prints. Verified by running it. That's why the lab just calls loc1.myLocation().

questions.text: The full myLocation.py runs to the end. What is its third line of output?
questions.context:
loc1 = Location("Tomas", "Portugal")
loc1.myLocation()
loc2 = Location("Ying", "China")
loc3 = Location("Amare", "Kenya")
loc2.myLocation()
loc3.myLocation()
your_loc = Location("Your_Name", "Your_Country")
your_loc.myLocation()
options: Hi, my name is Amare and I live in Kenya.
Hi, my name is Ying and I live in China.
Hi, my name is Your_Name and I live in Your_Country.
Hi, my name is Tomas and I live in Portugal.
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 3d: output follows the order of the method calls: Tomas, Ying, Amare, then Your_Name. Instantiating loc2 and loc3 prints nothing by itself. Verified by running it.

questions.text: A class can be instantiated as many times as you like, with different values for its variables each time.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 3: “Now that you have a class, you can instantiate it as many times as you like providing different values for the class variables each time.” loc1, loc2, loc3 and your_loc each keep their own name and country.

questions.text: How many methods does the Circle class have, counting __init__()?
questions.context:
class Circle:
    def __init__(self, radius):
        self.radius = radius
    def circumference(self):
      pi = 3.14
      circumferenceValue = pi * self.radius * 2
      return circumferenceValue
    def printCircumference(self):
      myCircumference = self.circumference()
      print ("Circumference of a circle with a radius of " + str(self.radius) + " is " + str(myCircumference))
questions.explanation: Part 5: “The class includes three methods including the __init__() function” — __init__(), circumference() and printCircumference().

questions.text: Match each Circle method to its job.
allChoices: Stores the radius value for the instance
Calculates the circumference and returns it
Builds and prints the result sentence

pairs.match: Stores the radius value for the instance
Calculates the circumference and returns it
Builds and prints the result sentence

questions.explanation: Part 5 notes: __init__() provides a method for entering the radius; circumference calculates the value and returns it (stored in circumferenceValue); printCircumference prints a string using it.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks so circumference() hands its result back, and printCircumference() calls it on the same instance.
questions.explanation: Part 5: circumference returns the value, and printCircumference calls it as self.circumference() — one method calling another on the same object.

questions.text: Why does printCircumference() wrap self.radius and myCircumference in str()?
options: They're numbers, and joining a number to a string with + raises an error
To round them to two decimal places
Because print() only accepts one argument
To convert them to integers
questions.explanation: Part 5: “Otherwise, the print statement would throw an error because self.radius and myCircumference are not strings.” Without it you get TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str — checked by running it.

questions.text: What does circle1.printCircumference() print for circle1 = Circle(2)?
options: Circumference of a circle with a radius of 2 is 12.56
Circumference of a circle with a radius of 2 is 6.28
Circumference of a circle with a radius of 2 is 12.566370614359172
Circumference of a circle with a radius of 2 is 4
questions.explanation: 3.14 * 2 * 2 = 12.56. The class uses pi = 3.14, not math.pi. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What does circle2.printCircumference() print for circle2 = Circle(5)?
options: Circumference of a circle with a radius of 5 is 31.400000000000002
Circumference of a circle with a radius of 5 is 31.4
Circumference of a circle with a radius of 5 is 31.40
Circumference of a circle with a radius of 5 is 15.7
questions.explanation: 3.14 * 5 * 2 is 31.400000000000002 in Python. 3.14 can't be stored exactly in binary, and the tiny error shows up here (not for radius 2 or 7). Verified by running the script; round(..., 2) would give 31.4.
questions.warning: The real output is 31.400000000000002, not 31.4 — floating-point rounding error.

questions.text: What does circle3.printCircumference() print for circle3 = Circle(7)?
options: Circumference of a circle with a radius of 7 is 43.96
Circumference of a circle with a radius of 7 is 21.98
Circumference of a circle with a radius of 7 is 43.982297150257104
Circumference of a circle with a radius of 7 is 153.86
questions.explanation: 3.14 * 7 * 2 = 43.96. 153.86 would be the area (π × 7²), not the circumference. Verified by running it.

questions.text: The Circle class's comment says c = pi * 2 * radius, but the code computes pi * self.radius * 2, so the code gives a different answer than the formula.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Multiplication order doesn't change the value: both are 2πr, the circumference formula (the script's header comment and Part 5's second note).

questions.text: The Circle class won't run because its method bodies are indented 6 spaces instead of 4.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Python only requires each block to be indented consistently, not by exactly 4 spaces. The script runs as written (verified). Four spaces is just the style convention.

questions.text: Match each term to its meaning.
allChoices: An independent, named block of code
A function that belongs to a class and is called through an object
A blueprint for creating objects with properties and methods
Creating an object from a class
The method that runs when an object is created

pairs.match: An independent, named block of code
A function that belongs to a class and is called through an object
A blueprint for creating objects with properties and methods
Creating an object from a class
The method that runs when an object is created

questions.explanation: Parts 2 and 4: a function is independently defined and called by name; a method depends on the object it's defined in; a class creates objects with properties and methods; instantiating creates one; __init__() is always initiated on instantiation.
